title: AlphaGo
subtitle: Deep neural networks and tree search for the game of Go
author: Lilith Learning Lab
description: A 12-chapter course on AlphaGo, the DeepMind program that beat a professional Go player and then Lee Sedol. Based on the 2016 Nature paper by Silver, Huang and colleagues and public accounts of the Fan Hui and Lee Sedol matches. Covers the rules of Go, Monte Carlo tree search before AlphaGo, the 48-plane input and the policy network, supervised learning from expert games, the fast rollout policy, policy-gradient self-play, the value network, the search with PUCT and mixed evaluation, hardware and Elo, a tic-tac-toe miniature, and the matches, successors and criticism. Python labs run on the built-in MicroPython engine. DeepMind did not release the code; the labs are teaching miniatures.

summary: AlphaGo is the DeepMind program that became the first to beat a professional Go player on a full board without handicap. It did so in October 2015 against the European champion Fan Hui, and in March 2016 it beat Lee Sedol, one of the world's top players, four games to one.

Its idea is to combine Monte Carlo tree search with deep neural networks. A policy network suggests promising moves, which cuts the breadth of the search. A value network judges positions, which cuts its depth.
The networks were trained in stages: first to imitate human experts, then improved by self-play. This course builds each piece in small Python programs.

keyPoints: AlphaGo was published in Nature on 28 January 2016 by Silver, Huang and colleagues at DeepMind.
It beat the European champion Fan Hui 5-0 in October 2015, the first win over a professional on a full board without handicap.
It beat Lee Sedol 4-1 in March 2016.
Four learned components: a fast rollout policy, an SL policy network, an RL policy network and a value network.
Policy networks cut the breadth of the search; the value network cuts its depth.
Later versions (Master, Zero) and AlphaZero removed the human data.

items: ELI5. AlphaGo is a computer that taught itself to play Go by combining two skills: an instinct for good moves and a way to look ahead. Like a player who feels where to play, then checks the idea by imagining the next few turns.

For decades Go was seen as the hardest classic game for computers. Chess programs conquered the human champion in 1997, when Deep Blue beat Garry Kasparov. In Go the strongest programs of the time had only reached about amateur five dan, and still could not beat a professional without a handicap.

The Nature paper of 28 January 2016, by David Silver, Aja Huang and eighteen colleagues, changed that. Its abstract introduces value networks to evaluate board positions and policy networks to select moves.

These deep neural networks are trained by a novel combination of supervised learning from human expert games and reinforcement learning from games of self-play. It also introduces a new search algorithm that combines Monte Carlo simulation with the value and policy networks.

The headline results: the program won 99.8 percent of its games against other Go programs, and defeated the human European Go champion by five games to zero. The champion was Fan Hui, a professional of rank two dan.
The match took place in October 2015, and the news was held back until the paper appeared in January 2016.

The sequel was a five-game match in Seoul in March 2016 against Lee Sedol, a nine dan professional. AlphaGo won four games to one, and was later awarded an honorary nine dan by the Korea Baduk Association.
Lee won the fourth game, the only loss AlphaGo suffered in its official games, a story told in chapter 12.

Here is the plan of the machine. A search must handle two problems. Go has about two hundred and fifty legal moves in a typical position and games last about a hundred and fifty moves, so the tree is enormous. The paper uses two general principles.
A value function lets the search stop early by judging a position directly, reducing depth. A policy lets it look only at likely moves, reducing breadth.

AlphaGo has four learned components. A fast rollout policy is a small linear model that plays quickly. A supervised learning policy network, called the SL policy network, is a deep convolutional network trained to predict the moves of human experts.
A reinforcement learning policy network starts from the SL network and is improved by self-play. A value network is trained to predict the winner of games played by that RL network against itself.

summary: Go is played on a 19 by 19 grid. Black and White alternate placing a stone on an empty point. Connected stones of one colour form a group, and the empty points next to a group are its liberties. A group with no liberties is captured and removed.

A move that repeats an earlier position is not allowed; this is the ko rule. At the end the players count area: a player's stones plus the empty points surrounded only by their stones. White receives komi, here 7.5 points, because Black moves first.
The rules fit on a page, but a typical position has about two hundred and fifty legal moves and a game lasts about a hundred and fifty moves.

keyPoints: Players alternate; Black moves first.
A group is captured when it has no liberties.
Suicide moves are generally forbidden and positions may not repeat (ko).
Chinese area scoring counts stones and surrounded empty points; the Lee Sedol match used a 7.5 komi.

Evaluating a Go position is hard because the board has no simple material count.

items: ELI5. Go is two players placing black and white stones to surround territory. The rules fit on a page, yet there are more positions than atoms in the universe. That is why brute force fails.

Go is about two thousand five hundred years old and is played on a grid of nineteen lines by nineteen. Two players, Black and White, take turns putting a stone of their colour on an empty intersection. Black plays first. Stones never move. Once placed they stay until captured.

Stones of the same colour that touch along a grid line form a group. The empty points that touch a group along grid lines are its liberties. When Black plays the last liberty of a White group, the group is captured and removed from the board.
A player may not make a move that leaves their own group with no liberties, unless that move captures something. This ban is called the suicide rule, and it varies slightly between rule sets.

Ko is the situation in which two players could capture one stone back and forth forever. Rules forbid a move that would recreate an earlier board position. Different rule sets phrase this differently, and the details matter in play.
The labs here implement the simplest version: you may not immediately recreate the position of one move ago.

The game ends when both players pass. Under Chinese rules, as used in the Lee Sedol match, each player scores their stones plus the empty regions that only they border. White adds komi because Black has the advantage of the first move.
The Lee match used seven and a half, and the half point guarantees there are no ties.

Now compare Go with chess in numbers from the paper. Chess has a branching factor of about thirty-five and a depth of about eighty. Go has a branching factor of about two hundred and fifty and a depth of about a hundred and fifty. Exhaustive search is hopeless in both, and Go is far worse.

The second difficulty is evaluation. In chess, counting material gives a useful first estimate of who is ahead. In Go every stone is worth the same, and the value of a position depends on the potential of groups, the ownership of regions and fine tactical fights.
Programmers had struggled for decades to write a good evaluation function by hand. That is what makes learning an evaluation function so attractive.

The practice section builds the fundamental operations on a small board: neighbours, groups and liberties, playing a move with captures, and area scoring. A board is a list of strings, one per row, with X for Black, O for White and a dot for empty.

chapters.title: Before AlphaGo: search and Monte Carlo

maps.title: Computer Go

summary: Chess programs search deeply with alpha-beta and a hand-written evaluation. In Go that approach stalled: the tree is too wide and no one could write a good evaluation. Programs stayed weak amateurs.

Progress came from Monte Carlo methods. To judge a position, play many random games from it and count the wins. Monte Carlo tree search builds a tree and spends more simulations on moves that look promising, with a bandit rule such as UCT choosing which to explore.
By 2015 the strongest programs, such as Crazy Stone and Zen, used MCTS and reached strong amateur level. AlphaGo's contribution was to guide that search with learned networks.

keyPoints: Hand-written evaluation functions for Go never reached strong play.

items: ELI5. Before AlphaGo, programs picked a move by playing thousands of random games from it and counting wins. It is like judging a restaurant by tasting random dishes. It worked a bit, but was weak.
For Go, the classical recipe failed. Alpha-beta search needs an evaluation to apply when it stops. In chess a short list of features gives a decent one.

In Go no one managed to hand-write an evaluation that worked, and the branching factor of two hundred and fifty means the search cannot go deep anyway. For many years the best programs played at weak amateur level.

The first breakthrough around 2006 was to give up on evaluation functions and estimate value by sampling. To judge a position, play many games from it using fast random or lightly guided moves until the end, and count how often each side wins. This is a Monte Carlo rollout.
With enough rollouts the win rate is a usable measure, even though each random game is a poor player.

The next step was to apply the sampling inside a tree. Monte Carlo tree search starts with just the current position as the root. Each simulation does four things. It selects a path down the existing tree. It expands a new node at the end of the path.
It plays a rollout from the new node to the end of the game. It backs up the result, updating win counts along the path. As simulations accumulate, the tree grows deeper along promising lines.

How to select? Treat each choice of move at a node as a slot machine arm. The UCB1 rule from the multi-armed bandit literature picks the arm with the best average reward plus a bonus that grows with the logarithm of the total plays and shrinks with the arm's own plays.
Applying this rule at every node of the tree is the UCT algorithm of Kocsis and Szepesvari. The dates and names here are my background knowledge, and the Nature paper cites this work.

By the time of the paper, the strongest open-source program, Pachi, which uses 100,000 simulations per move, was ranked at two amateur dan. Programs such as Crazy Stone and Zen were stronger. Yet even the best ones could not beat a professional without a handicap, a gap of many levels.

Rollouts have a hidden weakness. A random game is not like a real game, so its result can mislead: a position that looks equal to random play may be lost against good play. The remedy used by strong programs was to make rollouts smarter with local patterns.
AlphaGo keeps rollouts, with a small linear policy, but mixes them with a learned value, as chapter 9 shows.
The practice section builds the UCB score and a flat Monte Carlo evaluator on a simple stone-taking game, with a tiny deterministic random generator so that results are reproducible.

chapters.title: Looking at the board: features and policy networks

maps.title: Inputs and outputs
links: Policy network | takes | 48 planes of 19 by 19

summary: A neural network cannot read a board directly. AlphaGo turns each position into a stack of 19 by 19 binary planes: where the black, white and empty stones are, how recently each move was played, how many liberties each group has, and so on. The paper lists 48 such planes.

A convolutional network turns the planes into a probability for every point of the board. A final softmax makes the numbers positive and sum to one. Illegal moves are given probability zero by a mask before the numbers are renormalized.
This chapter builds the encodings and the softmax in code. The training comes in the next chapters.

keyPoints: The policy network input is 48 binary 19 by 19 planes; the value network adds a plane for the player's colour.
Planes include stone colour (3), turns since a move was played (8), liberties (8), capture size (8), self-atari size (8), liberties after move (8), ladder capture and escape, and sensibleness.
The output is a probability for each of 361 points.
Softmax: p_i = exp(z_i) / sum_j exp(z_j).
Illegal moves are masked out and the rest renormalized.
In search, the paper uses a softmax temperature of 0.67 on the SL policy network for priors.

items: ELI5. A policy network looks at the board like a picture and says which places look promising. It is a quick gut feeling, trained to point where a strong player would look first.

Think of a photograph. A photograph has three colour channels, each a grid of numbers. AlphaGo treats a Go position the same way. The board is a nineteen by nineteen image with many channels, and each channel is a yes-or-no map of one fact about the position.

The paper's list, in its Extended Data tables, has forty-eight planes for the policy network. Three planes give stone colour: points with the player's stones, the opponent's stones, and empty points. One plane is all ones. Eight planes record how many turns ago each stone was played.

Eight record how many liberties each group has. Others mark how many stones a move would capture, how many stones a move would put in atari, how many liberties a stone would have after it is played, and whether a ladder would capture or escape. One marks moves that are sensible.
The value network adds a plane for whose turn it is.

Why features instead of the raw board alone? The paper reports that using only the raw board position and the move history, the network reached 55.7 percent accuracy at predicting expert moves, against 57.0 percent with all features.
The extra planes help a little, as hand-written knowledge about liberties and ladders saves the network from having to discover them.

The network is a stack of convolutional layers, thirteen for the SL policy network. Each layer applies small filters, with rectifier nonlinearities between them. The final layer produces one score for each of the 361 points. A softmax turns the scores into probabilities.

Not all of the 361 points are legal. Some are occupied and some break the ko or suicide rules. The search should never consider them. A legal mask sets the probability of illegal points to zero and divides the rest by their total, so the result still sums to one.
One more knob: the temperature. If every probability is raised to a power below one and the result renormalized, the distribution flattens and makes rare moves more likely.

The paper applies a softmax temperature of 0.67 to the SL policy network when it produces priors for the tree search, to spread the search over more candidate moves. The exact transformation used in the practice section is my own simple version of the idea.
In the practice section you write the softmax, the legal mask, three stone planes and the temperature operation.

practice.title: Softmax
practice.intro: Write softmax(z): the list of exp(z_i) / sum of exp(z_j). Subtract the maximum first for numerical safety. Use import math.
practice.hint: Exponentiate the shifted scores and divide by their sum.
practice.solution:
import math
def softmax(z):
    m = max(z)
    e = [math.exp(x - m) for x in z]
    s = sum(e)
    return [x / s for x in e]

practice.intro: Write masked(p, legal): legal is a list of 0/1 flags. Zero the probability of illegal moves and renormalize the rest so they sum to 1. If nothing is legal return the zeros.

practice.title: Flatten the distribution

    q = [x ** beta for x in p]
    s = sum(q)
    return [round(x / s, 9) for x in q]

summary: The first training stage is plain supervised learning. Take positions from games played by strong humans on the KGS Go Server, and train the network to give high probability to the move the expert actually played.

The training signal is the log likelihood of the human move: the weights are nudged in the direction that makes that move more probable. In the paper, a 13-layer network trained on 30 million positions predicted the expert move 57.0 percent of the time, against 44.4 percent for the previous best.
The labs write the loss, its gradient and a full tiny training loop for a linear softmax model.

keyPoints: The SL policy network is trained to maximize the log likelihood of the human move.
Update: delta sigma is proportional to the gradient of log p_sigma(a | s) with respect to sigma.
For softmax outputs, the gradient of -log p_a with respect to the logits is p - onehot(a).
The paper: 13 layers, 30 million positions, 57.0 percent accuracy (55.7 percent from raw board and history only).
The earlier state of the art was 44.4 percent.
A stronger accuracy gave much stronger play, though the network was slower to evaluate.

items: ELI5. First the network learned by copying thousands of expert games, like an apprentice watching masters. Given a position, it guessed the master's move. This gave it good habits before it played anyone.

Stage one of AlphaGo is imitation. The training data are positions from the KGS Go Server, a site where strong amateurs play. The paper says the data set held 29.4 million positions from 160,000 games. For each position the label is the move the player actually chose, one of 361 points.

The network gives a probability for each point. The natural loss is the negative log of the probability given to the human move, called cross-entropy. If the network is sure about the right move the loss is near zero. If it gives the move a tiny probability the loss is large.
To train, compute the gradient of the loss and take a small step the other way. For the final softmax layer there is a neat result.

The gradient of minus log p of the correct action with respect to the scores, the logits, is just the vector of predicted probabilities minus a one-hot vector for the correct action. A move that was too unlikely gets pushed up and every other move gets pushed down in proportion to its probability.

The paper trained with stochastic gradient ascent on the log likelihood, which is the same thing as descent on the loss. After training, the 13-layer network predicted the expert move correctly 57.0 percent of the time using all features, and 55.7 percent with only the board and move history.
The best earlier result the paper cites was 44.4 percent. That sounds modest, but there are 361 candidate points and humans disagree with themselves.
A key finding was that small gains in accuracy led to large gains in playing strength. Bigger networks were more accurate but slower to evaluate.
The network's evaluation took a few milliseconds, which is why the paper also trains a much faster, weaker policy for rollouts, the subject of the next chapter.

Imitation has a ceiling. A network trained to copy humans plays like a blend of the humans in its data. To go beyond them, the paper adds a second stage in which the network improves through self-play, chapter 7. But the SL network remains useful in the final search.

The paper reports that the SL policy gives better priors to the tree search than the stronger RL policy, perhaps because humans pick a diverse set of promising moves while RL tunes onto a single best move.
The practice section writes cross-entropy, the accuracy metrics, the softmax gradient, one training step for a linear softmax model and a small training loop.

practice.title: One training step
practice.intro: A linear softmax model has weights W (a list of rows, one per move, each of the same length as the feature vector x). Write sgd_step(W, x, a, lr): compute logits z_i = sum_j W[i][j] * x[j], p = softmax(z), and return the new weights W[i][j] - lr * (p[i] - onehot[i]) * x[j]. Use import math.

import math
def sgd_step(W, x, a, lr):
    z = []
    for row in W:
        z.append(sum(w * v for w, v in zip(row, x)))

summary: The deep network is slow: several milliseconds per position. A Monte Carlo rollout needs a move at every step of a game that may last 150 moves. So AlphaGo trains a second, much smaller policy for rollouts: a linear softmax over small pattern features.
It picks a move in about 2 microseconds, about 1,500 times faster than the SL policy network, at the cost of accuracy: 24.2 percent against 57.0 percent.
A similar linear policy, the tree policy, supplies provisional priors for new tree nodes until the network has finished evaluating them.

keyPoints: The rollout policy p_pi is a linear softmax of small pattern features.
It reached 24.2 percent accuracy and takes about 2 microseconds per action.
It ran about 1,000 simulations per second per CPU thread on an empty board.

items: ELI5. Looking ahead needs speed. A small fast network and simple rules play out games quickly, like a sketch instead of a painting. Speed buys many more imagined games.

A Monte Carlo rollout plays a game to the end from a position. With about a hundred and fifty moves in a game, one rollout needs about a hundred choices. If each choice cost three milliseconds, as for the deep network, a single rollout would take a third of a second. The search needs thousands.
So a different tool is needed for that job.

The paper trains a fast rollout policy p pi. It is a linear softmax of small pattern features. For each legal move it computes features of the nearby stones, takes a weighted sum, and applies a softmax across moves.
The paper says it achieved 24.2 percent accuracy, against 57.0 percent for the big network, but needs only about two microseconds to select an action. That is about fifteen hundred times faster.

What are the features? The paper lists a set of small pattern features, including patterns of stones in a three by three neighbourhood around a move and some features about the last move and responses to it.

A three by three neighbourhood has eight surrounding points, each empty, black or white, so each local pattern can be given a single number by reading the eight points as digits in base three. The practice section builds that.
The linear model has so few computations that the paper reports about one thousand simulations per second per CPU thread on an empty board. This is the throughput a Monte Carlo search needs.
It was trained on 8 million positions from the Tygem server, with the same supervised method as the big network.

There is also the tree policy p tau. It has a similar structure but richer features. The paper uses it for a specific job: when the tree grows a new node, the network that supplies priors takes time to compute.
In the meantime, the tree policy gives provisional values, so the search is never blocked waiting for the network.
The trade is a general one in engineering search programs. A slow and accurate component is used sparingly, at the important decision points. A fast and crude component fills the bulk of the work.
AlphaGo uses the deep networks in the tree and the linear policy in the rollouts, then blends their opinions, chapter 9.
In the practice section you score moves with a linear softmax, encode a three by three pattern as a number, compute throughput and the speed ratio, and sample a rollout move deterministically.

summary: Imitation copies the experts' moves; it does not directly optimize winning. The second stage fixes that. The RL policy network starts as a copy of the SL network and plays games against earlier versions of itself, adjusting its weights to win.

The update is the policy gradient. After a game, every move played is made more likely if the game was won and less likely if it was lost: the weights move in the direction of the gradient of log p, multiplied by plus one or minus one.
The result was strong. The RL policy network won more than 80 percent of games against the SL network, and 85 percent against Pachi with no search at all.

keyPoints: The RL network is initialized to the SL weights (rho = sigma).
It plays against randomly selected earlier iterations, to avoid overfitting to the current self.
Update: delta rho is proportional to (d log p_rho(a_t | s_t) / d rho) times z_t.
The reward is +1 for a win and -1 for a loss; zero for all other steps.

items: ELI5. Then the program played against copies of itself and got better by rewarding wins. It is like practising chess against your own shadow and keeping whatever works. This went beyond its human teachers.

Supervised learning optimizes the wrong thing. It makes the network predict what a human would do, which is related to winning but not the same thing. The paper's second stage adjusts the policy toward the correct goal of winning games, rather than maximizing predictive accuracy.

The RL policy network p rho has the same structure as the SL network, and its weights rho start equal to the SL weights sigma. It then plays games against other versions. The paper says the opponent is a randomly selected earlier iteration of the network.
Using a pool of older versions stabilizes training and prevents overfitting to the current policy. The pool is refreshed every five hundred iterations.
Each game ends with a reward. The outcome z at the end is plus one for a win and minus one for a loss, and all intermediate rewards are zero. Now the learning rule.

For every position s t and move a t in the game, the weights move in proportion to the gradient of the log probability of the move, multiplied by the outcome z t of the game as seen by the player who made the move.

Read this carefully. If the player won, z is plus one, and the gradient is added: every move of the winning game becomes a bit more probable. If the player lost, z is minus one, and the gradient is subtracted: every move of the lost game becomes a bit less probable.
Some of those moves were good and some bad, but on average winners play better moves than losers. With many games, signal beats noise.

The scale was large. The paper reports training with mini-batches of 128 games, 10,000 of them, on 50 GPUs, for one day. The result, tested by play, was strong. Playing head-to-head, the RL policy network won more than 80 percent of games against the SL policy network.

Using no search at all, it won 85 percent of games against Pachi, the strongest open-source program, which ran 100,000 simulations per move. Earlier networks trained only by supervised learning won 11 percent against Pachi.

An important caution from the paper: when the strongest RL network was used to give priors in the tree search, AlphaGo played worse than with the SL network. The RL network was stronger alone but its use in the search was less helpful.
Where the RL network matters is the next stage: it generates the games from which the value network learns.

The practice section implements the REINFORCE update on a tiny softmax policy, the expected update when the game outcomes are known, a training loop that watches the policy shift toward winning moves, and the pool schedule.

import math
def expected_step(logits, zs, lr):
    m = max(logits)
    e = [math.exp(t - m) for t in logits]
    s = sum(e)
    p = [t / s for t in e]
    n = len(logits)
    out = []
    for j in range(n):
        g = 0.0
        for i in range(n):
            t = 1.0 if i == j else 0.0
            g += p[i] * zs[i] * (t - p[j])
        out.append(logits[j] + lr * g)
    return out

practice.intro: Repeat expected_step many times. Write train_bandit(zs, lr, steps): start from zero logits and apply the expected update steps times; return the probability of the first best action (the lowest index with the largest outcome) after training, rounded to 4 decimals.
practice.hint: Run the expected update in a loop; compute the softmax at the end.
practice.solution:
import math
def train_bandit(zs, lr, steps):
    n = len(zs)
    logits = [0.0] * n
    for k in range(steps):
        m = max(logits)
        e = [math.exp(t - m) for t in logits]
        s = sum(e)
        p = [t / s for t in e]
        new = []
        for j in range(n):
            g = 0.0
            for i in range(n):
                t = 1.0 if i == j else 0.0
                g += p[i] * zs[i] * (t - p[j])
            new.append(logits[j] + lr * g)
        logits = new
    m = max(logits)
    e = [math.exp(t - m) for t in logits]
    s = sum(e)
    best = 0
    for i in range(n):
        if zs[i] > zs[best]:
            best = i
    return round(e[best] / s, 4)

summary: The value network estimates the outcome of the game from a position: a single number between minus one and one. It is a deep network like the policy network, with one scalar output, and it takes an extra input plane saying whose turn it is.
Training it needed care. Positions from a single game are strongly correlated, and early attempts that used all positions from human games memorized the games and failed on new ones.
The fix was to generate 30 million positions, each from a different self-play game, and to regress them on the game outcomes.
The result approached the accuracy of Monte Carlo rollouts with the RL policy, with about 15,000 times less computation.

items: ELI5. A value network looks at a board and says how likely you are to win, like a referee glancing at a game and saying who is ahead. It saves playing every game to the end.

Now the part that gave AlphaGo its eye for positions. The value network v theta takes a board and predicts the outcome of the game for the player to move, between minus one for a sure loss and plus one for a sure win.
It has the same convolutional structure as the policy network, plus the player-colour plane, and ends in a single number.
The data are pairs: a position and the final result of the game it came from. Training is regression. The network's output should be close to the result, and the loss is the mean squared error.
A perfectly unsure network that always says zero has a squared error of one on every sample, since the result is plus or minus one. So an error below one means the network has learned something.

The obvious plan, training on positions from the human expert games, failed. The paper reports that the network memorized the game outcomes instead of generalizing: mean squared error 0.19 on the training set but 0.37 on the test set. The reason is correlation.
Successive positions in one game are nearly identical, and all share one result, so the network can recognize which game a position is from and recite the result.
The cure is to break the correlation. The paper generated a new data set by self-play with the RL policy network.

For each game, it picks one random time step u, plays the moves before u from the SL policy network, makes one random move at step u to add variety, and then plays on with the RL policy network until the end. Only the position at step u and the final outcome go into the data.
This produced 30 million positions, each from a separate game.

With that data the value network trained properly, with a mean squared error of 0.226 on the training set and 0.234 on the test set, little overfitting. The paper trained it with 50 million mini-batches of 32 positions on 50 GPUs for a week.
The result: a single evaluation of the value network approached the accuracy of Monte Carlo rollouts using the RL policy network, with about fifteen thousand times less computation.

The comparison is vivid. Before this, evaluating a position meant playing it out many times. Now one forward pass of the network gives a comparable answer. This is the second half of how AlphaGo shortens the search: the value network replaces deep lines of play by a single judgement.

summary: AlphaGo's search is Monte Carlo tree search with a twist: the networks guide it. Each edge of the tree stores a prior probability P from the SL policy network, a visit count N, and an average value Q.

Selection picks the move with the highest Q plus a bonus u that is large for moves with a big prior and few visits. When a leaf is reached it is expanded, then evaluated two ways: by the value network, and by a fast rollout. The two are mixed with weight one half each.
After the search the program plays the most visited move, not the one with the highest Q.

glossary.def: The policy network's probability for move a in position s.
How many simulations passed through the edge.
The mean of the evaluations of all simulations through the edge.
An exploration term, proportional to P divided by 1 plus N.
The weight on the rollout in the leaf evaluation; 0.5 in the paper.
A temporary penalty added to a path being explored, so parallel threads spread out.

keyPoints: Selection: a_t = argmax over a of Q(s_t, a) + u(s_t, a).
u = c_puct * P * sqrt(sum_b N(s, b)) / (1 + N(s, a)) with c_puct = 5 in the paper.
Leaf value: V = (1 - lambda) v_theta + lambda z, with lambda = 0.5.
Backup: N += 1 and Q becomes the mean of all V in the subtree.
A leaf is expanded when its edge has been visited 40 times (threshold n_thr = 40).
At the end, play the most visited move; resign if the win estimate falls below 10 percent.

items: ELI5. The search imagines moves, uses the policy to pick which to explore and the value to judge where they end. It is a detective who follows the best leads first and weighs the evidence at each.

The search is the heart of AlphaGo, where the four learned components meet. Each node of the search tree is a position. For each legal move from it, an edge stores three numbers. P is the prior probability of the move, supplied by a policy network.
N is how many simulations have passed through the edge. Q is the average value of the evaluations found beneath it.

Every simulation starts at the root and walks down the tree, at each node taking the action that maximizes Q plus a bonus u. The bonus is proportional to the prior and shrinks as the edge is visited more. Moves the network likes get explored first; moves visited often rely on their measured value.

lesson.tex: \begin{gathered} a_t \;=\; \arg\max_a\bigl(\, Q(s_t, a) + u(s_t, a)\,\bigr), \\[0.6em] u(s,a) \;=\; c_{\mathrm{puct}}\, P(s,a)\, \frac{\sqrt{\sum_b N(s,b)}}{1 + N(s,a)} \end{gathered}

items: The paper's methods give the constant c puct as five. The main text says only that u is proportional to the prior over one plus the visit count, and the fuller form with the square root appears in the methods.
This is the rule that AlphaZero later reused under the name PUCT, a variant of the UCT rule from chapter 3.

When a simulation reaches a leaf, the leaf is evaluated in two ways. The value network gives v theta of the leaf, and a fast rollout with the rollout policy plays the game to the end for a result z. The leaf value is a blend of the two.

The paper tested the blend. A version using only the value network, lambda equal to zero, reached an Elo rating of about 2,177, and the mixed version with lambda one half did best, with the two kinds of evaluation complementing each other: the value network is accurate on the position as a whole and the rollouts catch sharp tactical details.
The backup step then goes up the path. Each edge on the path gets its count N increased by one, and its Q set to the mean of all leaf values from the simulations that passed through it.
A detail to watch: Q must be seen from the viewpoint of the player who owns the edge, so the sign flips from level to level.

Other numbers from the methods. The SL policy network supplies the priors, with a softmax temperature of 0.67. A node is expanded only once its edge has been visited forty times; before that the cheaper tree policy provides the priors.

Parallel threads use a virtual loss of three to avoid all following the same path. In the end the program plays the most visited move at the root, and it resigns if its best estimated win probability drops below ten percent.

practice.intro: Write select(Q, N, P, cpuct): return the index of the edge maximizing Q[i] + cpuct * P[i] * sqrt(sum(N)) / (1 + N[i]); ties go to the smaller index. Use import math.
practice.hint: Compute Q plus the bonus for every edge and take the largest.
practice.solution:
import math
def select(Q, N, P, cpuct):
    root = math.sqrt(sum(N))
    best = -1e9
    arg = 0
    for i in range(len(Q)):
        s = Q[i] + cpuct * P[i] * root / (1 + N[i])
        if s > best + 1e-12:
            best = s
            arg = i
    return arg

summary: Strength in Go is measured with the Elo rating: a difference of 400 points means the stronger side is expected to win about 91 percent of the time. The paper's table gives a single-machine AlphaGo about 2,890 and the distributed version about 3,140, against 1,929 for Crazy Stone.

The distributed version used 1,202 CPUs and 176 GPUs in the match against Fan Hui. The paper also ran a tournament in which the single-machine version, with 48 CPUs and 8 GPUs, won 494 of its 495 games against other Go programs.
The search ran asynchronously: many threads walk the tree at once, while the networks are evaluated on GPUs in a batch behind them.

keyPoints: Elo: expected score = 1 / (1 + 10^(-d/400)); 400 points is about 91 percent.
Single machine: 40 search threads, 48 CPUs, 8 GPUs, Elo about 2,890.
Distributed: 40 search threads, 1,202 CPUs, 176 GPUs, Elo about 3,140.
Against other programs the single machine won 494 of 495 games with 5 seconds per move.
Distributed AlphaGo beat the single-machine version 77 percent of the time.
Mixed evaluation beat value-only and rollout-only versions.

items: ELI5. Strength came from computers as well as ideas: many machines, many chips. Elo is a score that says how likely you are to beat another player. More hardware gave more depth, with diminishing returns.

How strong is strong? The Nature paper answers with a tournament. It pitted AlphaGo against the best programs available: Crazy Stone, Zen, Pachi, Fuego and GnuGo, giving each five seconds per move. The single-machine AlphaGo won 494 out of 495 games, a winning rate of 99.8 percent.
Against four handicap stones it still won 77 percent against Crazy Stone, 86 percent against Zen and 99 percent against Pachi.

The paper converts results to Elo ratings, a scale in which a given rating difference corresponds to a given expected score. Distributed AlphaGo scored 3,140, single-machine AlphaGo 2,890, Crazy Stone 1,929, Zen 1,888, Pachi 1,298, Fuego 1,148 and GnuGo 431.
The distributed version won 77 percent of games against the single machine, which fits a difference of about 250 Elo.

Here d is the rating advantage, and E the expected score. A difference of zero gives one half. A difference of four hundred gives about ninety-one percent. The formula can be reversed to get the Elo difference implied by a winning rate, which the practice section does.

Now the engineering. The single-machine version used 48 CPUs and 8 GPUs, and forty search threads. The distributed version used 1,202 CPUs and 176 GPUs, again with forty search threads but with evaluation spread across machines.
The paper's largest test configuration reached 1,920 CPUs and 280 GPUs. The paper's table also shows the rating rising with extra GPUs on one machine, then flattening.

Parallel search raises a problem. If forty threads each pick the best edge at the same time, they all pick the same one. The remedy is virtual loss: when a thread passes through an edge, the edge temporarily looks worse by a few lost games, so the next thread is nudged to a different path.
When the evaluation returns, the penalty is removed and the real result is added.
The networks are slow, so the search does not wait for them. When a thread reaches a leaf, it requests an evaluation and continues.

The paper says that the evaluation of the policy network happens asynchronously on GPUs, while the search thread uses the quick tree policy for provisional priors, then updates them when the network answers. Rollouts, by contrast, run on the CPUs.
In the practice section you convert between Elo and win rates, build a rating table, compute the cost of the rollouts, and decide handicaps from rating differences.

summary: This chapter puts the pieces together on tic-tac-toe, small enough to run in a lab. The prior comes from a hand-made rule instead of a policy network, the value network is a stub that always says zero, and the rollouts use a tiny random generator.
Everything else follows the paper: PUCT selection with constant five, a leaf value mixing value and rollout, a sign flip in backup and the most-visited move at the end.
It is a teaching miniature, not DeepMind's program. Its purpose is to show that the loop of chapter 9 is short to write.
Build it in steps: result detection, prior, rollout, then the full search.

A new leaf is evaluated as 0.5 * v + 0.5 * z with v = 0 here.
z is the outcome of a random rollout from the leaf's player-to-move view.

items: ELI5. The capstone builds a tiny AlphaGo on a small board. The same parts, a gut feeling, a judge and a careful search, at toy size so you can see every step.

Time to build. The game is tic-tac-toe, played on a board of nine characters, X, O or a dot. It has no hidden depth, but it has everything the search needs: legal moves, terminal positions and sign flips between the players.

Start with the prior. A real AlphaGo asks the SL policy network. We use a hand-made table that favours the centre, then the corners, then the edges. After a softmax over the legal moves it plays the role of the probabilities P. Next, the value network.
A trained one is out of reach in a lab, so the stub value is zero, meaning no opinion. The rollouts do the real work, and the mixing weight one half applies to the zero.
The rollout is a random game played from the leaf to the end. We use the same small generator as in chapter 3, so the results are repeatable.
The outcome z is scored from the point of view of the player to move at the leaf: plus one if that player eventually wins, minus one if they lose, zero for a draw.

The search itself is a loop. In each simulation, walk down from the root. At each node already in the tree, apply the PUCT rule to choose a move, using the stored visit counts and values. At the first new node, create it, compute its priors, evaluate it with the mixed value, and stop.
If the walk reaches a finished game, score it exactly. Then walk back up, adding one to each count and the value to each total, flipping the sign each time.

The sign flip deserves attention. A value is always stored from the viewpoint of the player who plays the edge. A good result for the child node, where the opponent moves, is a bad result for us. So when passing a value up one level, negate it.
Forgetting this is the commonest bug in tree-search code.

At the end the visit counts at the root are the answer. With enough simulations the winning moves collect most of the visits. The most visited move is played, following the paper. The program is far too small to play Go, but the same loop with a real network and a Go simulator is what AlphaGo does.
In the practice section you first write the board helpers and the prior, then the rollout, and finally the whole search, comparing it with a position where the win is easy to see.

summary: The first AlphaGo, later called Fan, beat Fan Hui 5-0 in October 2015. A stronger version, Lee, beat Lee Sedol four games to one in March 2016. Lee won game four after a move, number 78, that the program had not anticipated.

Master, an updated version, won 60 straight online games in late December 2016 and early January 2017, and in May 2017 beat Ke Jie 3-0. AlphaGo Zero then learned Go from self-play alone, without human games, and beat the Lee version 100-0.
Critics pointed to the huge computing cost, the reliance on human data in the first versions, and the narrowness of Go as a test of intelligence.

items: ELI5. AlphaGo beat a world champion in 2016, and later versions learned without human games. Critics ask about cost, narrow skill and what it teaches about general intelligence.

The first public match was in secret. In October 2015 the distributed version of AlphaGo played Fan Hui, the European champion and a professional of two dan, in five games. It won all five. It was the first time a Go program had beaten a professional without handicap on a full board.
The news was held until the Nature paper appeared on 27 January 2016.

Then came Seoul. From 9 to 15 March 2016, AlphaGo played Lee Sedol, a nine dan professional, in five games under Chinese rules with seven and a half points komi. The prize was one million US dollars, to be donated to charities.
AlphaGo won games one, two and three, each by resignation, so the match was decided after three games.

Game two is remembered for move 37 by AlphaGo, a surprising shoulder hit that commentators found strange at first; this is widely reported but is not covered in the sources that I used here. Game four is remembered for Lee Sedol.

He won by resignation at move 180, and his move 78 is often called the divine move. Afterwards Aja Huang explained that AlphaGo's networks had not expected that move and so the program failed to adjust, a weakness the team patched. Game five went to AlphaGo, for a final score of four to one.
Lee Sedol said after the match that he had misjudged the program's abilities and that the loss was not a defeat of mankind. AlphaGo received an honorary nine dan from the Korea Baduk Association.

Fan Hui, by contrast, described the program's style as conservative, and the referee of his match said the same. Strategists noted that AlphaGo prized probability of winning over the size of its lead, so it often chose safe moves that won by little.

Next versions. In late December 2016 and early January 2017, an account named Master, later confirmed to be an updated AlphaGo, won sixty games without a loss against top professionals online, including three against the top-ranked Ke Jie.
In May 2017 at the Future of Go Summit in Wuzhen, Master beat Ke Jie three games to nothing. AlphaGo was then retired.

Then the Zero line removed the human data. AlphaGo Zero, published in October 2017, learned from self-play alone. After three days it surpassed the Lee version, winning a hundred games to none, and after forty days it exceeded all earlier versions.
AlphaZero, in December 2017, applied the same idea to chess and shogi as well as Go. The AlphaZero course in this library covers it.

Criticism and caveats. The original needed expert game records, so it depended on human knowledge. Its hardware was large: a cluster of CPUs and GPUs, or by one account 1,920 CPUs and 280 GPUs for the Lee match. It needs a perfect simulator of the rules to search.
Go is also only one game, and doing well at it does not by itself show general intelligence. Lee Sedol retired in 2019, saying that AI dominance meant he could never be the top overall player.

What changed in the world? Professional players studied AlphaGo's moves and revised long-held opening habits. Fan Hui, who lost to it, said the experience taught him to see things he had not seen before, and his ranking climbed afterwards.
A film about the preparation for the Lee match, directed by Greg Kohs, was released.
